projects.oneliner: I rebuilt the live Shopify store of a US shooting-sports retailer.
projects.summary: I rebuilt the live Shopify store of a US shooting-sports retailer that sells through paid ads. I moved 1,276 products with zero errors and no broken landing pages, and set up its Printify apparel line.
projects.problem: The store sells about 1,100 shooting and outdoor products, mostly to visitors from paid ads. On a phone, old collection pages showed a banner and a block of text before any product. projects.outcome: Live since 16 September 2026. On the test store before launch, my speed fixes took the new homepage's mobile Lighthouse score from 36 to 70. I removed a 3.35 MB development script and delayed video loading on phones. I also wrote alt text for 975 products.

projects.title: PoliClean Services bilingual website
projects.role: Sole developer: design, build, hosting setup, DNS move and handover
projects.oneliner: Seven-page English and French site for a family cleaning company in Quebec.
projects.summary: A seven-page English and French website for a family cleaning company in Quebec, built with React on Cloudflare Pages. Each estimate request is saved to a database and emailed to the owner, so no lead is lost if the email fails.
projects.problem: PoliClean is a family cleaning business in Vaudreuil-Dorion, Quebec, with customers who speak English or French. The owners are often out on jobs, so the site had to collect requests they could answer later. Their Google Workspace email already ran on the domain and could not go down.
projects.built: A seven-page React and Vite site with all text in English and Québec French, switched with one tap. The estimate form posts to a Cloudflare Pages Function that saves the lead to D1 and emails it through Resend. The form has a honeypot, a five-per-hour limit and header-injection stripping. Our Work has drag-to-compare before/after sliders.
projects.hard: I moved the DNS from Squarespace to Cloudflare while the business kept receiving mail through Google Workspace. I checked the mail records first, and the site sends from a separate subdomain, so the MX records were never touched. The database write and the email run separately, so if one fails the lead is kept.
projects.outcome: It runs on the client's own GitHub and Cloudflare accounts, with a README and a maintenance runbook. Every push to main deploys through GitHub Actions. I still make changes on request, with 18 commits between 9 September and 6 October 2026. Traffic and leads have not been measured.

projects.role: Sole developer, from written spec to hand-over
projects.status: Delivered; live in the owner's own accounts, private behind sign-in
projects.oneliner: Offline phone app for a family farm, including medication withdrawal dates.
projects.summary: A phone app for a family farm. It records animals, treatments, medication withdrawals, breeding and births in a barn with no signal, and syncs when signal returns. I delivered it six days after the first commit.
projects.problem: A family farm with rabbits, sheep, goats and poultry needed records it could update from an iPhone in a barn with little signal. Some records have legal weight. A medication withdrawal date decides when meat or milk can leave the farm. The spec ran to 59 sections, and the app had to run on free tiers in the owner's own accounts.
projects.built: A React and TypeScript web app that installs to the home screen. Every screen reads a local copy of the data, so it works the same online or offline. Saves go into an ordered queue that uploads to Supabase when signal returns, and a banner counts the changes still waiting. The database enforces Owner, Editor and Viewer roles.
projects.hard: Offline saves had to be safe. Records get their IDs on the phone, so a weight logged for an animal created offline links to it before the server has seen either. The queue uploads strictly in order and sets aside a change that keeps failing, so it can't block the rest. Withdrawal dates are time-zone safe.
projects.outcome: Delivered on the agreed date, six days after the first commit, into the owner's own Supabase and Cloudflare accounts. The app syncs when it is open and has signal. The client's public 5.0 review: "Very good communication and worked quickly."

projects.title: Sorare Trading Bot
projects.role: Sole developer: design, build, live validation, VPS deployment and documentation
projects.status: Maintained; runs in Docker on the client's VPS
projects.oneliner: Bot that watches a live card market 24/7 and alerts Discord.
projects.summary: A Python bot for a Sorare trader. It watches the live card market 24/7 and posts underpriced listings to Discord. In a 24-hour test run it checked 588,748 market events and missed none.
projects.problem: The client trades football and NBA cards and wanted to hear about a mispriced listing within seconds. The market sends every event over a WebSocket, but the raw feed needs filtering. Of the settlements, 57% are expiries that look exactly like sales, and sellers leave cards listed at prices nobody pays. The documented rate limits were also wrong.
projects.built: A Python asyncio service reads the stream, keeps price baselines in SQLite and checks every listing against the client's rules, each with its own Discord channel. The client edits rules with slash commands and a 5-step wizard, and changes apply on the next event with no restart. It deploys with one docker compose up -d.
projects.hard: The API's real rate limit didn't match its documentation, so I measured it. One key and three rotated keys were refused the same 16.7% at 300 players a minute, so the limit is per account. Stepping up the rate found the real ceiling, 200 calls a minute. A token-bucket scheduler with cheapest-first checks cut API demand by 91%.
projects.outcome: In a 24-hour run from an empty database, it never restarted and dropped no events. Alerts reached Discord a median 0.46 s after listing. It made 166,926 API calls at 76% of the budget with no rate-limit refusals. It runs on the client's VPS today.
projects.result: In a 24-hour test it missed none of 588,748 market events and alerted Discord a median 0.46 s after listing.
highlights: Asyncio service on a GraphQL WebSocket stream, with price baselines per player
Alert rules edited from Discord with slash commands and a 5-step wizard, no restart

projects.title: BugsInPy Audit
projects.role: Sole developer: extractor, environment builder, run pipeline, validator and reports
projects.oneliner: Reproducible audit of 501 Python bugs, with evidence for every verdict.
projects.summary: For a PhD researcher, I built a reproducible pipeline that extracts, rebuilds and re-tests all 501 bugs in the public BugsInPy benchmark. Each bug has an evidence-backed verdict: 476 confirmed, 19 unconfirmed, 6 not reproduced.
projects.problem: BugsInPy is a public benchmark of 501 real bugs from 17 Python projects. For each bug, the researcher needed to know whether the buggy code can be cut out exactly as it was before the fix, and whether it fails before the fix and passes after in a fresh run. The old environments no longer install cleanly.
projects.built: My extractor uses Python's ast module to read source from git objects and find the smallest complete function or class around each change. An environment builder recreates each bug's exact interpreter. A resumable runner tests the buggy and fixed versions and records a verdict with an evidence path. Finally, a validator re-checks every row, file and checksum offline.
projects.hard: A provenance check compares every extracted file with the blob the patch names. It caught six defects in the benchmark's own data. Running the other 495 bugs showed four faults in the existing harness, which had blocked 26 of them. I applied each fix only after the client approved its exact sha256.
projects.outcome: All 501 bugs have a recorded outcome. With the original harness, 90.5% of 495 bugs reproduced. With its four faults fixed, 95.2% did, a total that matches the 95% a 2023 study reached with a different toolchain. A second extraction matched the first on all 2,540 files.
projects.result: 476 of 501 bugs confirmed, each with its evidence. Fixing four harness faults raised the reproduced share from 90.5% to 95.2%.
highlights: ast-based extractor reading straight from git objects
Rebuilds each bug's exact interpreter from conda-forge lock files or a CPython source build
Resumable runner with a time limit per bug, recording a verdict and evidence path for each one
Offline validator with a self-test of 109 deliberately broken fixtures
Provenance check that caught six defects in the benchmark's own data

projects.title: TuniCompare
projects.status: Live; the hosted demo runs on a historical price snapshot (August 2025)
projects.oneliner: Real-time price comparison across three Tunisian retailers that share no product codes.
projects.summary: A real-time price comparison site for laptops, desktops and screens across three Tunisian retailers. It scrapes each store and matches listings for the same product without a shared ID. The hosted demo runs on a historical snapshot (August 2025).
projects.problem: Comparing a gaming laptop's price in Tunisia means opening three store sites. Each describes the same machine with different titles, field names, units and spellings, and none share a product code.
projects.built: A Python pipeline feeds a Flask site. Three scrapers use regular expressions to pull CPU, GPU, RAM, storage and screen specs out of product titles. A loader puts them into one format per category, and a matcher pairs each Tunisianet product with its closest Mytek and Scoop Gaming listing. The site shows three prices side by side, cheapest highlighted.
projects.hard: Each candidate pair gets a fuzzy title score plus a spec check written for its category, and only pairs above a threshold count as the same product. Conflicting specs reject a pair, and an offer bundled with Windows counts as a different product. Specs are normalized first, so the check compares actual values.
projects.outcome: After fixing the matcher, I labelled every matched pair by hand. Laptop precision is 0.98 (145 of 148), up from 0.525 on a sample of 40 before the fix. Desktops and screens are both at 1.00. The 2025 scrape holds 1,278 listings, and in October 2026 I moved the site to Vercel.
projects.result: After I fixed the matching, laptop precision rose from 0.525 to 0.98. I checked every matched pair by hand.
highlights: Three scrapers pulling specs out of free-text product titles
Category-specific spec comparison plus fuzzy title scoring to match products

projects.title: Telegram Calendar Assistant
projects.oneliner: Telegram bot that uses AI to turn plain messages into Google Calendar events.
projects.summary: A Telegram bot that manages Google Calendar from plain messages. A language model turns "meeting with Ali tomorrow at 2 PM" into a real event. I also built a Telegram AI chat bot with memory.
projects.problem: Calendar apps make you fill in forms. I wanted to type "I'm meeting my friend Ali tomorrow at 2 PM" into Telegram, see it appear in Google Calendar, and then change or cancel it the same way. Most of the work is turning the model's free-text reply into calls that change a real calendar.
projects.built: The bot is a python-telegram-bot app. /connect runs Google's OAuth2 consent once and refreshes the token when it expires. Every other message goes to a language model through OpenRouter with a strict prompt. It asks for one of four actions (create, list, update, delete) plus title, place and local times. The bot parses that reply, calls the Google Calendar API and keeps history in SQLite.
projects.hard: A small model's output had to be safe to act on. The prompt allows only four actions. It forces "N/A" for anything the user didn't say and "Error" when a request is too vague, so a vague message changes nothing. For updates and deletes, the bot looks the event up by title first and refuses if nothing matches.
projects.outcome: A working prototype with public code. In the recorded demo, creating, moving, listing and deleting events all work. While recording it in October 2026, I fixed three bugs: moving an event to another day, timezone offsets, and a false "created" reply. It runs on my machine and is not hosted.
projects.result: Create, move, list and delete all work in the recorded demo. It's a prototype that runs on my machine, not hosted.

projects.title: Axiom (axiom-ml)
projects.status: Prototype: 0.1.1 on PyPI, 0.1.2 on GitHub main
projects.oneliner: A machine-learning library written from scratch in NumPy, published on PyPI.
projects.summary: I wrote a machine-learning library in Python and NumPy with no ML framework, published on PyPI as axiom-ml. It has neural networks with hand-written backpropagation, plus linear and logistic regression. Version 0.1.2 on GitHub adds decision trees and gradient boosting.
projects.problem: I wanted to see each step of training, including every gradient and weight update and why the starting weights matter. With no autograd, nothing catches a wrong derivative, so training just drifts and you have to find out why.
projects.built: The package needs only NumPy and installs with pip install axiom-ml. It has neural networks (Dense and activation layers, four losses, momentum, L2, automatic He, Xavier or LeCun initialisation), linear and logistic regression, decision trees, gradient boosting, optimisers, scalers and encoders. XGBoost-style and LightGBM-style boosters and linear trees are modules I'm building.
projects.hard: I wrote backpropagation by hand. When a sigmoid output feeds binary cross-entropy, the combined derivative reduces to (prediction − target) / batch size, and the model detects that pairing and uses the short form. I tested the maths against known answers. A linear layer must land on the normal-equation solution, and a small sigmoid network must learn XOR.
projects.outcome: First commit to PyPI release took just over three weeks. In my benchmark on small datasets, predict calls ran 8× to 64× faster than scikit-learn (0.1.1, median of five seeds), because they skip scikit-learn's input checks. Fitting the linear models is slower, and gradient boosting in 0.1.2 predicts about 7× slower.
projects.result: In my benchmark (0.1.1), predict calls ran 8× to 64× faster than scikit-learn on small datasets, because they skip its input checks.
highlights: Backpropagation derived and written by hand, with no autograd
Checked against known answers: closed-form least squares, XOR, a TensorFlow reference

projects.title: Marcaria TLD Scraper
projects.oneliner: Selenium scraper that collects 1,183 domain extensions from a Cloudflare-protected site.
projects.summary: For a client, I built a Python scraper that collects the domain extensions sold on Marcaria.com, with each one's registration link and eligibility rules, from pages behind Cloudflare's bot check. The delivered list holds 1,183 unique extensions.
projects.problem: The client needed Marcaria's catalogue of domain extensions, with each one's eligibility rules, as a spreadsheet. The site is behind Cloudflare's bot check and the catalogue is split into three sections. An extension's rules only appear in a pop-up after a click.
projects.built: Three Selenium scrapers, one per section, run Chrome through undetected-chromedriver so it passes the bot check like a normal visitor. For every extension marked as having requirements, the country and generic scrapers open the pop-up and read its text with BeautifulSoup. A merge script then combines the results into one CSV without duplicates.
projects.hard: The rules aren't in the page source. They only load into a pop-up after a real click on the requirements link. So the scraper scrolls the link into view, sends a mouse event and checks the pop-up for up to 20 seconds. When Cloudflare shows "Just a moment", it waits instead of failing the run.
projects.outcome: The delivered file lists 1,183 unique extensions. Of these, 326 carry the registry's eligibility rules as text, from local-presence and citizenship rules to trademark routes.
projects.result: Delivered a CSV of 1,183 unique domain extensions from a Cloudflare-protected site, 326 with the registry's eligibility rules as text.
highlights: Passes Cloudflare's bot check with undetected-chromedriver and waits out challenge pages
Click-triggered pop-ups read with real mouse events and 20-second polling

projects.title: Competition record
projects.role: Entrant at DataLeaders 2.0 and Orbyx; team member at Roboday 4.0
projects.status: Placements confirmed; all three were in-person events with results announced on site
projects.oneliner: 1st at DataLeaders 2.0, Top 5 at Orbyx, 2nd at Roboday 4.0.
projects.summary: In my first year at ENSI I placed 1st of 30+ at DataLeaders 2.0 with a three-layer stacking ensemble, Top 5 at the Orbyx ML Challenge, and 2nd of 60+ at Roboday 4.0 with a robotics team.
projects.problem: All three were in-person events with results announced on site. DataLeaders 2.0 and the Orbyx ML Challenge were machine-learning competitions, and Orbyx asked entrants to classify planets as livable or not. Roboday 4.0 was a robotics event.
projects.built: For DataLeaders 2.0 I built a three-layer stacking ensemble: XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost as base models, and a meta-model combining their predictions. For Orbyx I wrote a custom classifier. At Roboday 4.0 I was on a robotics team.
projects.hard: In stacking, several kinds of model make predictions and a meta-model combines them. I built mine for DataLeaders, to a deadline, in a ranked competition.
projects.outcome: DataLeaders 2.0 (January 2026): 1st of 30+, Grand Prize, with accuracy 9% above the other competitors and more than 30% above the baseline models. Orbyx ML Challenge (November 2025): Top 5, accuracy 20% above baseline. Roboday 4.0 (November 2025): 2nd of 60+.
projects.result: Placed 1st of 30+ at DataLeaders 2.0, with accuracy 9% above the other competitors.
highlights: 1st place and Grand Prize at DataLeaders 2.0 with a stacking ensemble
Top 5 at the Orbyx ML Challenge with a custom classifier
2nd place at Roboday 4.0 with a robotics team
Also competed at the DataQuest hackathon, with a FastAPI app around a gradient-boosted model
